cards.title: Starship's first full test flight ends in an explosion
cards.body: SpaceX launched its Starship rocket, booster and ship stacked together, for the first time from Starbase in Texas. Several booster engines failed, the two stages did not separate, and the vehicle was destroyed about four minutes after liftoff. The launch also badly damaged the launch pad.

cards.title: Starship's second flight: stages separate, both are lost
cards.body: On its second test flight, Starship's booster and ship separated successfully using 'hot staging', where the ship's engines ignite before separation. The booster broke apart soon after, and the ship was lost later in its climb, before completing its planned flight path.

cards.title: Starship reaches space on its third flight
cards.body: Starship's ship stage reached its planned path through space for the first time and tested opening its payload door and moving propellant between tanks. It broke up while re-entering the atmosphere over the Indian Ocean, and the booster was lost before its planned splashdown.

cards.title: Both Starship stages survive for the first time
cards.body: On the fourth test flight, the Super Heavy booster made a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico and the ship survived re-entry to make a controlled splashdown in the Indian Ocean. It was the first flight on which both stages came back down intact.

cards.title: Launch tower catches a returning Starship booster
cards.body: On Starship's fifth test flight, the Super Heavy booster flew back to the launch site and was caught in mid-air by two mechanical arms on the launch tower, nicknamed 'chopsticks'. It was the first time a booster had been caught this way. The ship made a controlled splashdown in the Indian Ocean.

cards.title: Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time since 2018
cards.body: The US Federal Reserve raised its target for the federal funds rate by a quarter of a percentage point, to 0.25-0.5%. It was the first increase since 2018 and the start of a series of rises aimed at bringing down high inflation.

cards.title: Fed lifts rates to their highest level in 22 years
cards.body: The Federal Reserve raised its federal funds target range to 5.25-5.5%, the highest level in 22 years. It was the eleventh increase since March 2022 as the central bank kept pressure on inflation.

cards.title: Federal Reserve cuts rates by half a point
cards.body: The Federal Reserve lowered its federal funds target range by half a percentage point, to 4.75-5%. It was the first cut since 2020. The Fed said it had gained greater confidence that inflation was moving towards its 2% goal, and that risks to jobs and to inflation were now roughly in balance.

cards.title: India's three new criminal law bills become law
cards.body: After Parliament passed them in December 2023, the President gave assent to three bills that replace India's colonial-era criminal laws: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam. A later date was set for them to take effect.

cards.title: India's new criminal laws come into force
cards.body: From 1 July 2024, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code of 1860, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure of 1973, and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam replaced the Indian Evidence Act of 1872.

cards.title: India win the 2024 T20 World Cup
cards.body: India beat South Africa by seven runs in the final in Barbados to win the ICC Men's T20 World Cup. It was India's second T20 world title, after the first edition of the tournament in 2007.

cards.title: US signs the CHIPS and Science Act into law
cards.body: President Joe Biden signed the CHIPS and Science Act, which provides about $52.7 billion for US semiconductor manufacturing, research and workforce programmes, aimed at making more computer chips in the United States.

cards.title: SpaceX
cards.body: SpaceX is a US rocket and spacecraft company founded by Elon Musk in 2002. It builds the Falcon 9 rocket, whose first stage lands and flies again, the Dragon spacecraft, and the Starlink satellite network. In 2020 it became the first private company to fly astronauts to the International Space Station.

cards.title: Why rockets need to go sideways, fast
cards.body: Getting to space is not mainly about height. To stay in low Earth orbit, a spacecraft must move sideways at about 7.8 km per second, so it keeps falling towards Earth but keeps missing it. Most of a rocket's fuel goes into building up that sideways speed.

cards.title: Reusable rockets: why landing boosters matters
cards.body: Most rockets are thrown away after one launch. Reusable launch vehicles bring parts back to fly again, aiming to cut the cost of reaching space. The hard part is returning a stage that is moving very fast and high up, slowing it down and landing it safely.

cards.title: First landing of an orbital rocket's booster
cards.body: On 21 December 2015, after launching satellites, the first stage of a SpaceX Falcon 9 flew back and landed upright at Cape Canaveral, Florida. It was the first time the first stage of a rocket launching to orbit had landed this way.

cards.title: The Space Race begins with Sputnik
cards.body: The Space Race was a Cold War contest between the Soviet Union and the United States. It began when the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, on 4 October 1957, and peaked when Apollo 11 landed the first humans on the Moon on 20 July 1969.

cards.title: Federal Reserve
cards.body: The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States, created by the Federal Reserve Act of 1913. Its Federal Open Market Committee sets the target for the federal funds rate. Congress has given it two main goals: maximum employment and stable prices.

cards.title: How interest rates steer the economy
cards.body: Central banks set short-term interest rates. Raising them makes borrowing more expensive, which slows spending and helps bring inflation down. Cutting them makes borrowing cheaper, which supports spending and jobs. The effects take time, often many months, to show up.

cards.title: Inflation: when money buys less
cards.body: Inflation is a general rise in prices across an economy, so each unit of money buys less than before. It is usually measured with a price index, such as a consumer price index that tracks a basket of everyday goods and services.

cards.title: Supply and demand
cards.body: In a market, the price of a good tends to settle where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer. If demand rises while supply stays the same, the price tends to rise; if supply rises while demand stays the same, the price tends to fall.

cards.title: Comparative advantage: why countries trade
cards.body: David Ricardo argued in 1817 that two countries can both gain from trade even if one is better at making everything. Each should focus on what it gives up least to produce. His example: England making cloth and Portugal making wine, then trading.

cards.label: Opinion
cards.title: Keynesian view: recessions come from too little spending
cards.body: Keynesian economists, following John Maynard Keynes, argue that recessions happen when total spending in the economy falls short. Their answer is for governments and central banks to step in, through public spending, tax cuts or lower interest rates, to restore demand and jobs.

cards.label: Opinion
cards.title: Austrian view: recessions correct earlier mistakes
cards.body: Economists of the Austrian school, such as Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek, argue that interest rates held too low cause booms built on bad investments. In their view the recession that follows is a needed correction, and government intervention mostly delays or worsens it.

cards.label: Opinion
cards.title: Case for cutting rates sooner
cards.body: People who favour earlier cuts argue that rate changes work with long delays, so waiting until inflation is fully at target risks keeping borrowing costs high for too long. That, they say, can cause unnecessary job losses once inflation is already falling.

cards.label: Opinion
cards.title: Case for holding rates higher for longer
cards.body: People who favour holding rates higher argue that cutting too early risks inflation coming back, as happened in the 1970s, and that a central bank losing credibility on inflation can end up having to raise rates even more later.

cards.title: The French Revolution
cards.body: The French Revolution began in 1789 and overturned France's absolute monarchy. Crowds stormed the Bastille prison in Paris on 14 July 1789, a date now France's national day. The revolution abolished feudal privileges, declared the Rights of Man and later executed King Louis XVI in 1793.

cards.title: The Industrial Revolution
cards.body: From about 1760 to the 1830s-1840s, Britain moved from hand production to machines, steam power and factories, starting with textiles. The changes spread to Europe and North America and transformed how and where people worked.

cards.title: The Partition of India
cards.body: In August 1947, British India was divided into two independent countries, India and Pakistan. The partition displaced millions of people, with estimates commonly ranging from about 12 to 20 million, and was accompanied by large-scale violence.

cards.title: The Berlin Wall falls
cards.body: On 9 November 1989, East Germany opened its border crossings and crowds began to cross and tear down the Berlin Wall, which had divided the city since 1961. Germany was reunified the following year, on 3 October 1990.

cards.title: The Indus Valley Civilisation
cards.body: A Bronze Age civilisation in today's Pakistan and northwest India, at its height from about 2600 to 1900 BCE. Its cities, such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, had planned streets and drainage systems. Its script has not been deciphered.

cards.title: The Maurya Empire
cards.body: Founded by Chandragupta Maurya around 322 BCE, the Maurya Empire came to rule most of the Indian subcontinent. Its best-known ruler, Ashoka, turned to Buddhism after the bloody Kalinga war and spread his ideas through edicts carved on rocks and pillars.

cards.title: The Roman Republic
cards.body: By tradition, Rome became a republic in 509 BCE after overthrowing its kings, with elected magistrates and a Senate in place of a monarch. The Republic lasted until 27 BCE, when Augustus became Rome's first emperor.

cards.title: The Battle of Marathon
cards.body: In 490 BCE, an Athenian army, helped by soldiers from Plataea, defeated a Persian invasion force at Marathon, northeast of Athens. The victory ended the first Persian invasion of Greece.

cards.title: Cricket's powerplay
cards.body: In a men's T20 international, the first six overs of each innings are the powerplay: only two fielders may stand outside the 30-yard circle. With the field pulled in, batters try to score quickly, so fast starts often decide T20 matches.

cards.title: Strike rate: how fast a batter scores
cards.body: A batter's strike rate is the average number of runs they score per 100 balls faced. A batter with 45 runs from 30 balls has a strike rate of 150. In short formats like T20, a high strike rate matters as much as the total.

cards.title: India win the first T20 World Cup
cards.body: India, captained by MS Dhoni, beat Pakistan by five runs in the final of the first ICC World Twenty20 in Johannesburg, South Africa.

cards.title: India win the 1983 Cricket World Cup
cards.body: Captained by Kapil Dev, India beat the two-time champions West Indies by 43 runs in the final at Lord's in London to win their first Cricket World Cup.

cards.title: Football's offside rule
cards.body: An attacker is in an offside position if, in the opponents' half, they are nearer the goal line than both the ball and the second-last defender when a teammate plays the ball to them. Being in that position is not an offence by itself; it is penalised only if they get involved in play.

cards.title: Expected goals (xG)
cards.body: Expected goals estimates how likely a shot is to score, based on many past shots with similar features such as distance and angle. A shot with an xG of 0.3 is scored about 30% of the time. Adding up a team's xG shows the quality of chances it created.

cards.title: How a bill becomes law in the US
cards.body: A bill is introduced in the House or the Senate and reviewed by committees. Both chambers must pass the same text. The President then signs it or vetoes it; Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both chambers.

cards.title: CHIPS and Science Act (2022)
cards.body: Status: in force. Signed in August 2022, this US law funds semiconductor manufacturing, research and workforce training, with about $52.7 billion for chips, plus support for science and technology research. Its aim is to make more advanced chips in the US.

cards.title: The First Amendment
cards.body: Status: in force since 1791, as part of the Bill of Rights. It bars Congress from establishing a religion or limiting its free exercise, and protects freedom of speech, of the press, to assemble peacefully, and to petition the government.

cards.title: How a bill becomes law in India
cards.body: A bill can start in either house of Parliament, the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha, except money bills, which must start in the Lok Sabha. After both houses pass it, it becomes law when the President gives assent. A deadlock over an ordinary bill can be settled at a joint sitting of both houses.

cards.title: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
cards.body: Status: in force since 1 July 2024. India's main criminal code, replacing the Indian Penal Code. It keeps much of the old code's structure, and adds changes such as community service as a punishment for some minor offences and separate offences for terrorism and organised crime.

cards.title: The Indian Penal Code of 1860
cards.body: The Indian Penal Code was drafted by British India's first Law Commission, chaired by Thomas Babington Macaulay, enacted in 1860 and in force from 1862. It remained India's main criminal code until the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced it in 2024.

cards.title: Right to Information Act, 2005
cards.body: Status: in force. Any Indian citizen can ask a public authority for information, which must usually be supplied within 30 days, or within 48 hours where a person's life or liberty is involved.

cards.title: Fundamental Rights in India's Constitution
cards.body: Part III of the Constitution (Articles 12 to 35) sets out six groups of Fundamental Rights: equality, freedom, protection against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and the right to go to the Supreme Court to enforce them (Article 32).

cards.label: Opinion
cards.title: Supporters: new laws replace colonial-era codes
cards.body: The government and supporters present the three new laws as replacing codes written under British rule with Indian ones focused on justice for victims, adding time limits for steps in investigations and trials, and making more use of technology such as electronic records.

cards.label: Opinion
cards.viewpoint: Critics, including opposition parties and some legal experts
cards.title: Critics: much is renamed rather than reformed
cards.body: Critics, including opposition parties and some lawyers, argue that much of the old text was carried over with new names and numbering, that the switch causes confusion for courts and police, and that some provisions give police wider powers.
